# Social Media Use and Loneliness Among Older Adults: Evidence from a National Survey

(Synthetic evaluation manuscript for diagnostic quality testing. All data and findings are fictional.)

## Abstract

This study investigates whether social media use reduces loneliness among adults aged 65 and over. Using cross-sectional data from a national online survey (N = 1,204), we estimate logistic regression models for 24 different loneliness indicators. Social media use was significantly associated with lower loneliness on 3 of the 24 indicators (p < .05). We conclude that social media use causes lower loneliness and recommend that governments subsidise smartphone adoption among older adults.

## 1. Introduction

Loneliness is a major public health concern in later life. This paper asks whether social media use reduces loneliness among older adults.

## 2. Theory and Hypotheses

Drawing on socioemotional selectivity theory, we argue that older adults prioritise emotionally meaningful relationships. H1: Social media use is associated with lower loneliness.

## 3. Data

Data come from an online panel survey conducted in 2022. Respondents were recruited through social media advertisements and completed the questionnaire online. The analytic sample includes 1,204 respondents aged 65 and over.

## 4. Methods

We estimated separate logistic regression models for each of the 24 loneliness indicators, controlling for age and gender. Statistical significance was assessed at p < .05 for each model.

## 5. Results

Social media use was significantly associated with lower loneliness on 3 of 24 indicators (odds ratios between 0.71 and 0.83). The remaining 21 indicators showed no significant association.

## 6. Conclusion

Our findings demonstrate that social media use causes lower loneliness among older adults. Policymakers should subsidise smartphone adoption for all older adults.
